summary:
Space telescopes capture huge amounts of sky data. It is public and free, but few people ever see it, because it is hard to find and comes in specialised formats.

CHALLENGER5 is our answer: an open web application that makes NASA's SPHEREx data easy to explore. Enter a name or coordinates and blink through the images of that spot in time order, so objects that move or change brightness stand out. A second slider tunes through 102 infrared channels, from 0.75 to 5.0 µm.

Our deep analysis is a handy tool for making changes visible: it compares the images over time and shows in a single picture where something moved.

This way anyone, not only experts, can help search the sky for moving objects like Planet X.
details: Space missions observe the sky every day, and the data is public and free, but few people ever see it: most don't know it exists, and those who do face huge files in specialised formats. CHALLENGER5 is our answer, an open web application that makes SPHEREx data accessible. You enter sky coordinates or a target name, and the app finds the available SPHEREx images covering that position and plays them in time order, so objects that move or change brightness stand out. What makes it creative is that it combines two dimensions in one simple interface: change over time and the spectral information of SPHEREx's 102 channels from 0.75 to 5.0 µm. You can blink through the observing seasons at one wavelength, or sweep through the wavelengths within one season. A deep analysis view adds difference images between observing seasons, where a moving star leaves a red mark at its old position and a blue one at its new position, and a spectrum for any pixel you click. All of this works in the browser, without having to download or process astronomical files manually, so students, hobbyists and researchers can explore the data and help make discoveries. We built it with Python, FastAPI and astropy in the backend, Angular in the frontend, PostgreSQL as a cache and Docker, using SPHEREx data from NASA's IRSA archive and its AWS copy. We focused on ease of use and speed, and the app reads the list of available datasets from the archive instead of hard-coding it, so new observations are picked up. Next, we want to host the app publicly, make it faster and add more analysis tools.
